newsitem.title: USA: Selenium supplements may block some cancers.
newsitem.headline: Selenium supplements may block some cancers.

text.p: Researchers investigating whether selenium can prevent skin cancer issued an unrelated finding on Tuesday that dietary supplements of the trace element may cut the risk of getting lung, colon and prostate cancers.

Midway through their planned 15-year study on skin cancer, researchers at the University of Arizona at Tucson found selenium supplements of 200 micrograms daily did nothing to stop recurrences of skin cancer but did reduce the incidence of the three other types of cancer by 37 percent. Mortality rates related to those cancers were 50 percent lower.

"The results of this study are exciting because they show the cancer prevention potential of a nutritional supplement to a normal diet," Arizona epidemiologist Larry Clark wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

The mineral, found in varying amounts in the soil whence it makes its way into the food chain, helps prevent blood clotting and maintains tissue elasticity that slows the ageing process. A toxic dose, estimated at more than 350 milligrams, can be deadly and can cause baldness, fatigue and loss of nails and teeth.

The study found taking selenium supplements did nothing to prevent reappearance of basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas, the most common forms of skin cancer, and also did not reduce the number of cancers of the bladder, neck, head or breast.

Clark added a cautionary note about his study's conclusions that was echoed by other cancer researchers, who called for a detailed trial to test the possible health effects of taking selenium supplements.

"For now it is premature to change individual behaviour, to market specific selenium supplements, or to modify public health recommendation based on the results of this one randomized trial," Graham Colditz of Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School wrote in an accompanying editorial.

Anti-cancer properties of selenium have been studied since the 1960s with mixed results. It was added to fertiliser in the mid-1980s In Finland to enrich selenium-poor soils, but there was no effect on rates of either cancer or cardiovascular disease.
Selenium is a trace element in meat, fish, whole grains, dairy products and vegetables, which usually provide the recommended allowance of 70 milligrams a day for men and 55 milligrams for women.

The Arizona study originally recruited 1,312 people who had suffered with skin cancer and lived in the eastern United States where relatively low selenium levels in the soil lower the amount of the mineral in foods raised there.

The subjects, who had a mean age of 63 years at the start of the study in 1983, were divided into two groups, one of which took a placebo and the other the supplements. It did not show any adverse effects from taking extra selenium.
